title: Rahul Vohra: The ₹144 Crore LinkedIn Exit That Taught Him Balance
excerpt: The British-Indian Superhuman co-founder sold Rapportive to LinkedIn for a reported $15 million months after collapsing from exhaustion. The health crisis rewired how he builds companies — and he has meditated twice daily ever since.
body:
• Rahul Vohra, the British-Indian co-founder of email startup Superhuman, sold his first company Rapportive to LinkedIn in 2012 for a reported $15 million (about ₹144 crore) — months after collapsing from stress-induced exhaustion.
  • He credits transcendental meditation — 30 minutes each morning and afternoon — for the calm, focused leadership that let him build Superhuman into an $825 million company.
  • For diaspora professionals in high-pressure tech and startup roles: his story is a concrete case for treating recovery like a business metric — he says this time around, burnout never entered the equation at Superhuman.
  • Superhuman was acquired by Grammarly in July 2025; Grammarly then rebranded the whole company as "Superhuman," and Vohra now leads its mail division.

Rahul Vohra was 27 when his startup Rapportive was being acquired by LinkedIn — and his body was already breaking down. The Gmail plugin he had co-founded two years earlier was a genuine hit: millions of users, a spot in Y Combinator, and a buyer in LinkedIn. Behind the scenes, the team was running on fumes. Months before the deal closed in February 2012, Vohra collapsed on a workday and was hospitalised the next day, with doctors linking the episode to years of poor eating, no exercise and relentless pressure. LinkedIn paid a reported $15 million — roughly ₹144 crore — for the company. The exit, in Vohra's telling, was never the hard part. Surviving it was.

Context & Background

Vohra grew up in Birmingham, England, the son of two doctors, and taught himself to code from the age of eight. He studied computer science at Cambridge, started a machine learning PhD, and dropped out after about 18 months to build products rather than research them. Between that exit and Rapportive, he tried six or seven startups that went nowhere. Before all of that, he spent a summer at game studio Jagex, where the RuneScape quest he designed — "Monkey Madness I" — became one of the most beloved in the game's history, still played two decades later.

Rapportive's premise was elegant: open an email in Gmail and a sidebar would show the sender's LinkedIn profile, tweets and recent activity — context without switching tabs. Vohra built the first working prototype in about six weeks. Getting into Y Combinator over Skype was itself an exception to the rule of in-person interviews. But the acquisition was no clean glide path: LinkedIn agreed to buy the company and then tried to back out, and with weeks of runway left, Vohra drip-fed product updates and monetisation evidence to the deal team to keep it alive. He closed the sale with roughly two weeks of cash remaining.

Impact & Analysis

The health scare reshaped how Vohra operates. He stepped away, recovered with family, and rebuilt his routine around food, exercise and transcendental meditation — 30 minutes every morning and 30 minutes every afternoon, a habit he still keeps. In 2014 he founded Superhuman with Conrad Irwin and Vivek Sodera, designing email software the way he once designed games: obsessed not with features but with how the product made people feel. Speed was philosophy, keyboard shortcuts were the game's controls, and onboarding was the tutorial level. The company became the defining cult productivity tool of its era, raising $118 million and reaching an $825 million valuation in 2021. His 2018 First Round Review essay on measuring product-market fit became the publication's most-shared article ever. Crucially, he says the second run carried none of the existential dread of the first — the company was growing fast and was not running out of money.

"When you make a game, you don't worry about what users want or need. You obsess over how they feel. That fundamental shift — from features to emotions — is what most software gets wrong."

— Rahul Vohra, Superhuman co-founder

Diaspora Angle

Vohra's arc lands differently for Indian-origin professionals abroad: the immigrant-family script of outworking everyone else is the very habit that hospitalised him at 27. For the large share of the diaspora in tech, finance and startups, his story makes the case in concrete terms — meditation twice daily, deliberate recovery, saying no to burnout — that stamina is a design choice, not a character trait. It is also a success story that started in a Birmingham library and ran through Cambridge and Silicon Valley without a single safety net of name or network.

What's Next

In July 2025, Grammarly acquired Superhuman in a deal estimated at $300–$500 million, and three months later rebranded the entire combined company as "Superhuman" — a sign the acquired brand had more equity than the acquirer's. Vohra now leads Superhuman Mail inside an entity with 40 million-plus daily active users and over $700 million in annual revenue. His current project is an AI-native productivity suite combining Superhuman Mail, Grammarly's writing assistance and an AI companion. If his second act proved burnout was optional, his third is testing whether one leader's philosophy of craft can scale across the whole surface of knowledge work.

nri_angle: Vohra's Birmingham-to-Silicon-Valley arc, and his public break with the diaspora's outwork-everyone script, give Indian-origin professionals in high-pressure roles a concrete founder-tested case for designing stamina instead of burning through it.
